cards.no: Ho voglia is the go-to; non me la sento implies a deeper reluctance.
Cavarsela = to manage/get by. Ce la siamo cavata is warmer and more colloquial.
Lascia perdere (forget it) is stronger — use it when you want to drop something entirely.
Sono in ritardo is neutral fact; sto arrivando reassures the other person you are moving.

cards.en: Can you do me a favour
cards.no: Mi dai una mano (give me a hand) is the more casual, everyday version.
Ci penso io implies you are taking ownership; ci devo pensare means you genuinely need time.

cards.en: I can get used to that
cards.no: Mi ci posso abituare — the ci refers back to the situation; locals almost always include it.
Divertirsi is reflexive — use divertitevi for a group, divertiti for one person.

cards.no: Past participle agreement: lasciato stays masculine here since the object (it) is unspecified.

cards.en: She got used to the new schedule

cards.no: Reflexive past always needs essere + agreement — abituata if the speaker/subject is female.

cards.en: It won’t let me do it / It stops me doing it
cards.no: Fare + infinitive is the causative — “non me lo fa fare” is the natural version, more common than “non mi lascia.”

cards.en: I took my clothes off / I got undressed
cards.no: Reflexive past + essere; togliersi i vestiti is a bit literal — spogliarsi is the go-to verb for getting undressed.

cards.en: There’s no feeling like being here

cards.ex: Non c'è niente di meglio che stare qui
cards.no: Added “qui” to complete the thought; “non c’è niente come...” is actually the more natural way to say this.

cards.en: In front of us / Ahead of us
cards.no: Davanti a and di fronte a are interchangeable for “in front of” — davanti a is the more everyday choice.

cards.en: The way he/she does things / His/her manner
cards.no: “Modo di fare” describes someone’s general manner/attitude, broader than just “style.”

cards.en: How long before we go? / When do we pass through?
cards.no: “Fra quanto” = “in how long” — the standard way to ask about timing.

cards.en: I didn’t think it would be this easy

cards.no: Conditional-in-the-past (sarebbe stato) is correct — corrected from “sarrebe.”
“Deluso da te” stays neutral; “mi hai deluso” shifts focus onto the action — both natural.

cards.en: Who knows who he/she learned it from

cards.no: Future of probability (avrà imparato) expresses a guess about the past — very common construction.
Potrebbe is plain possibility; rischia di adds a sense of danger.

cards.en: It’s already cleaner than this, what more do you want?

cards.ex: È già pulitissimo, cosa vuoi di più
cards.no: “Cosa vuoi” tacked on the end works as a rhetorical shrug — very colloquial.
Plural of indizio; prove is stronger — actual proof vs. a hint or clue.

cards.en: I think so / It seems likely
cards.no: “Mi sa” is the casual, gut-feeling version of “I think”; corrected si → sì (needs the accent for “yes”).

cards.en: You don’t have to pretend to be happy

cards.en: It feels good here / One feels at ease here
cards.no: Impersonal “si” construction — describes a general feeling of comfort in a place.
Capovolta works as an adjective (upside down) or a noun for the flip/somersault itself.
Corrected tenativo → tentativo; “ci hai provato” praises the effort itself rather than the result.
“Storica” here means “long-time,” not literally historical — common in casual Italian.

cards.en: Are you taking the piss? / You’re kidding me!
cards.no: Vulgar/informal register — prendere in giro is the polite equivalent with the same meaning.

cards.en: I haven’t seen Marco for two weeks

cards.en: I haven’t seen Marco for two weeks
cards.it: È da due settimane che non vedo Marco
cards.ex: Non vedo Marco da due settimane
cards.no: Fronting “è da...” puts more emphasis on the duration than the plain “da” version.

cards.en: He/it must have taken a really long time

cards.no: “Metterci” + time is the idiom for “it takes [someone] [time]”; dovere + past infinitive expresses a strong guess.

cards.no: Non-human subject (an app, a system) doing the blocking — bloccare covers literal and figurative stopping.

cards.en: There are more than 3,000 of them
cards.no: “Ce ne sono” = existential “there are” + “ne” replacing the counted item — don’t drop the “ne.”
Sdraiarsi and stendersi both mean “to lie down”; stendersi feels a touch more casual.
“Ecco come ragiono io” sounds more natural in conversation than the noun form.

cards.en: It would have taken me a whole morning to do it

cards.ex: Mi ci sarebbe voluta una mattinata intera
cards.no: Corrected mattina → mattinata — mattinata frames it as a whole morning span, not just “morning” generically.
Causative fare + infinitive; costringere implies more force/pressure than the neutral causative.
Near-synonyms; malinteso leans slightly more toward a communication mix-up.
Disagio is broader (physical or social unease); imbarazzo is specifically embarrassment.

cards.en: Leave me alone / Let go of me
cards.no: Mollare here = “let go/drop it”; imperative + “mi” attached, informal tone.

cards.it: Mi si stanno ancora sviluppando le orecchie.
cards.ex: Le mie orecchie si stanno ancora sviluppando.
cards.no: Indirect object construction (mi... le orecchie) is more natural than leading with the possessive.

cards.en: Can you tell me how it works?
cards.no: Restructured — “mi sai” needs “dire” right after it; sapere here means “are you able to.”

cards.en: Jordan is a pain / a drag
cards.no: Corrected the English possessive to “è”; “una rottura (di scatole)” and “una palla” both mean someone annoying.
Corrected spacing/apostrophe from “C’è ne tanto” — ne attaches directly after ce, no space.
Both common; “parliamo d’altro” is a touch more casual/deflecting.

cards.en: I’ll take care of him too
cards.no: Occuparsi di and pensare a both mean “to look after”; occuparsi sounds a bit more formal/responsible.
Vulgar exclamation — infame intensifies bastardo, implying particularly despicable behavior.

cards.en: I’m coming right away to open up
cards.no: Corrected aprirsi → aprire — non-reflexive here since you’re opening something (a door); venire a + infinitive needs “a.”
Andarsene is reflexive + “ne”; “già” sits between the auxiliary and the past participle.
Guardare (watch actively) and vedere (catch/see) are both used for watching sports.

cards.en: Who do you think will win?
cards.no: “Pensare che” + future indicative is common in casual speech, even though “credere che” formally wants the subjunctive.

cards.ex: Mi è arrivata una chiamata persa
cards.no: “Perdere una chiamata” is the direct, everyday way to say it.

cards.it: Mi sposto; Lo spostiamo qui?; Spostiamolo, qui dà fastidio.
cards.no: Reflexive spostarsi — used both literally (shifting position) and for stepping aside.

cards.ex: L’importante è che tu stia bene
cards.no: “Basta che” + subjunctive (stia) — a condition being sufficient always triggers the subjunctive.

cards.en: Let’s go for a little walk
cards.no: Giretto (diminutive of giro) makes it sound short and casual.

cards.en: In my view, I have my doubts
cards.it: Nel mio punto di vista, ho i miei dubbi
cards.ex: Secondo me, ho i miei dubbi
cards.no: Corrected visto→vista and miei→i miei; “secondo me” is actually the more natural way to say “in my view.”

cards.en: Everyone asks me this question. Everyone asks me it.

cards.ex: Me la fanno sempre, questa domanda.
cards.no: Second sentence swaps to chiedere + double clitic (me lo) — the natural way to avoid repeating “questa domanda.”
Direct object “lo” attaches before spostare — present tense used for an immediate near-future action.
Added the accent; “si è fatto buio” is the standard impersonal way to describe darkness falling.

cards.ex: Chi se ne occupa, dei dinosauri?
cards.no: Occuparsi di = “to be in charge of/deal with” a topic or field.

cards.en: I knew you would say that
cards.ex: Lo sapevo che l’avresti detto tu
cards.no: Conditional perfect (avresti detto) expresses “would say/would have said” from a past viewpoint.
Comportarsi is reflexive; needs a completion (e.g. “ti comporti bene/male”) to be a full sentence — incomplete as captured.

cards.en: Willing to stay here for kisses.
cards.it: Disposta a stare qui per dei bacini.
cards.ex: Disposto a stare qui per dei bacini (if speaker is male)
cards.no: “Disposta” is feminine — switch to “disposto” if the speaker is male.

cards.en: I make an effort to speak Italian every day.
cards.it: Mi sforzo di parlare italiano ogni giorno.
cards.ex: Cerco di parlare italiano ogni giorno.
cards.no: Sforzarsi di + infinitive — reflexive, always takes “di” before the verb.

cards.en: Make a bit of an effort.
cards.no: Imperative of the reflexive sforzarsi — “un po’” softens it into a friendly nudge rather than a demand.

cards.en: Climbing in the heat is demanding.
cards.it: Salire con il caldo è impegnativo.
cards.ex: Salire con questo caldo è una faticaccia.
cards.no: Impegnativo = demanding in effort/commitment, not just physically tiring.

cards.en: With this heat it’s really tiring.
cards.it: Con questo caldo è davvero faticoso.
cards.ex: Con questo caldo ti stanchi subito.
cards.no: Faticoso describes the activity as tiring, contrasting with impegnativo (more about effort/commitment).
Pungere (sting/bite) is the verb for insects — mordere is for mammal bites.

cards.en: The mosquitoes are eating me alive!
cards.no: Massacrare here is hyperbolic/informal — “eating me alive,” not literal.
“Ne” stands in for the noun already mentioned — don’t drop it or the sentence sounds incomplete.

cards.en: I've got the rest / I'll cover the rest
cards.no: Both mean “I’ll take care of it” — pago io implies money specifically, ci penso io is more general.
“Proprio quello che pensavo” is the more natural reaction in conversation than the literal version.
“Quanto pesa” (lit. how much does it weigh) is just as common and a bit more casual.
“Grande” covers both size and age depending on context.
“Quanto dista” is more formal/precise — “quanto è lontano” is what you’d actually say.

cards.en: I didn't imagine the park was so big
cards.it: Non immaginavo quanto fosse grande il parco
cards.no: “Quanto fosse” triggers the subjunctive because it follows a verb of thought/imagination.
“Ma quanto pesa!” is the more exclamatory native version — same idea, more emphasis.

cards.en: I'll tell you all about it later, I have to finish this now
cards.it: Poi ti racconto tutto quanto, adesso devo finire questo
cards.no: “Tutto quanto” = “the whole thing” — adds emphasis over plain “tutto.”

cards.en: I'll tell you later about something that made me laugh
cards.it: Poi ti racconto una cosa che mi ha fatto ridere
cards.no: “Poi ti racconto” is a stock conversational opener — use it to park a story for later.

cards.en: By the end of these next few weeks, I want to be able to speak naturally
cards.it: Entro la fine di queste settimane voglio riuscire a parlare in modo naturale
cards.no: “Riuscire a” = to manage to — implies real progress, stronger than just “potere.”

cards.en: I got it wrong before — the correct dates are October 1st to the 9th
cards.it: Prima avevo sbagliato, le date giuste ora sono dal primo ottobre al nove
cards.no: “Dal... al...” is the standard way to give a date range.

cards.en: I didn't expect that from you
cards.no: “Aspettarsi” (to expect) is reflexive — “me l’aspettavo,” not “l’aspettavo.”
Same reflexive verb, third person — “se lo aspettava,” not “lo aspettava.”
“Infatti” here means “actually/indeed,” confirming a suspicion — like saying “I called it.”

cards.ex: Si è appena resa conto (if she realized)
cards.no: “Rendersi conto” is reflexive and needs gender agreement in the past — reso (m) / resa (f).

cards.en: I just got it / understood it
cards.no: Simple non-reflexive past — contrast with “rendersi conto” above.

cards.ex: Voglio fare un giro in bici
cards.no: “Fare un giro in bici” (go for a bike ride) sounds more like a leisurely outing.

cards.en: To have crushed it (e.g. an exam)
cards.no: “Polverizzare” (lit. to pulverize) is slang for totally crushing/destroying something.
Informal imperative of “correggere” — add “se sbaglio” to soften it into a common request.

cards.en: We have to throw it away
cards.no: “Buttare via” (throw away) is more explicit than plain “buttare.”
“Quotidiano” = daily/everyday — think “day-by-day.”

cards.en: Sometimes people say you have a natural talent
cards.it: A volte la gente dice che hai un talento naturale
cards.no: “La gente” is always singular — “la gente dice,” not “dicono.”

cards.en: Well, it didn't seem very easy to me
cards.it: Beh non mi è sembrato molto facile
cards.no: “Sembrare” takes an indirect object — “mi è sembrato,” literally “it seemed to me.”

cards.en: I would really like to go to the beach
cards.it: Mi piacerebbe molto andare al mare
cards.no: It's “andare al mare” (to the sea), not “andare il mare” — al = a + il.
“In bici” = by bike — same construction as “in macchina,” “in treno.”

cards.en: Yesterday I went for a 100km bike ride
cards.it: Ieri ho fatto un giro in bici di 100 km
cards.no: “Un giro” = a ride/loop — sounds like a deliberate outing vs. the flatter statement above.
“Mancare” flips the subject — literally “this was missing to me.”
“Sagra” = a local food festival named after the star ingredient — common all over Italy.
“Dimenticare” needs the full verb; the reflexive “non dimenticarti di me” is an equally common alternative.
“Loro” (their) always goes with the article — “la loro personalità,” not just “loro personalità.”

cards.en: I want to give you some kisses
cards.no: “Dei baci” = some kisses — “dei” is the plural partitive article, like “some.”
Stock casual response to brush something off.
It's “tutte e due” (both, feminine) — for mixed/masculine, “tutti e due.”

cards.en: You can't go wrong with a t-shirt
cards.it: Non si sbaglia mai con una maglietta
cards.no: Impersonal “si sbaglia” = “one is wrong” — reads more natural than a literal translation.

cards.en: What was the weather like yesterday?
cards.no: Imperfect tense (faceva) because it describes an ongoing state in the past.

cards.en: What will the weather be like tomorrow?
cards.no: Future tense (farà) — same “fare” verb across all three weather questions.

cards.en: If you want, we're free now
cards.no: “Ci siamo” here means “we're around/available,” not literally “we are here.”
“Qual” drops the final “e” before “è” — never write “quale è.”
“Una cosa così” is the more casual, everyday version of the same idea.
“Dell'acqua” = some water, the partitive “di + la.”

cards.en: Let's go before it gets dark
cards.no: “Prima che” always triggers the subjunctive — “faccia,” not “fa.”

cards.en: I would have bought it because my girlfriend wanted one
cards.it: L'avrei comprato perché la mia ragazza ne voleva uno
cards.no: “Ne voleva uno” = “wanted one (of them)” — “ne” replaces the noun already mentioned.
“Sedersi” is reflexive — “posso sedermi,” not “posso sedere.”

cards.it: Vorrei tanto che tu fossi qui.
cards.ex: Mi sarebbe piaciuto che tu fossi qui (I'd have liked you to be here)
cards.no: Both trigger the subjunctive after “che” — “vorrei tanto” is the punchier, more common way to say it.

cards.en: Would you have liked to be here?
cards.no: Past conditional of “piacere” — plain infinitive here since the subject doesn't change.

cards.en: Would you have liked to listen?
cards.no: “Sarebbe piaciuto” is a notch more polite/soft than “avresti voluto” (you would have wanted).
Present conditional versions of the pair above — same soft/direct contrast, just not about the past.

cards.en: Could you pass me the salt? (casual)
cards.no: Present tense used as a casual request among friends/family — no need for the conditional.

cards.en: Could you please pass me the salt? (formal)
cards.it: Mi potrebbe passare il sale, per favore?
cards.no: Formal “Lei” conditional — use with strangers, waitstaff, elders.
Direct imperative — most casual of the three, fine with close friends/family.

cards.en: Can you open the door for me? (casual)
cards.no: Same casual-present-as-request pattern as the salt example.

cards.en: Could you please open the door for me? (formal)
cards.it: Mi potrebbe aprire la porta, per favore?
cards.no: Formal register pair to the casual door request.
Specifically the reusable kind (metal/plastic) — “bottiglia” is for a disposable bottle.
Common connector to link two parts of a story — “e dopo di che...”

cards.en: What do you say — of course not
cards.no: “Che dici” here is rhetorical, not really asking an opinion — more like “come on.”

cards.en: Could I have a glass of water?
cards.no: “Potrei” (could I) is softer/politer than “posso” (can I) — good default for restaurant requests.

cards.en: Excuse me, could I sit here? (formal)
cards.no: “Mi scusi” is the formal “excuse me” (Lei form) — “scusa” would be informal.
Common sympathetic reaction to bad news, not angry.
“Lasciare” + infinitive = “let (someone) do something” — pronoun attaches to the imperative.
Diminutive of “pensiero” (thought) — a small, no-big-deal gift, often said while handing it over.

cards.en: You know what we should do
cards.no: “Dovremmo” (conditional of dovere) is softer than “dobbiamo” — more like “we ought to.”
“Da quando” literally asks “starting when” — for just the departure time, “a che ora parte” is more direct.
“Mancare” (to be missing/lacking) — same verb family as “mi è mancato” (I missed it).
Object pronouns go before the conjugated verb — “la conosci,” not after.
Watch the spelling — “mesi” (months), not “messi.”
“Sentito male” = heard badly/wrong, not “felt bad” — context makes it about hearing.
“Ultimissima” is the superlative of “ultima” — “the very last.”

cards.it: Questo è successo prima che ci incontrassimo
cards.no: “Prima che” + subjunctive again — “incontrassimo,” not “incontrammo.”

cards.en: There's a ton of rain / it's raining a lot
cards.no: “Piove un sacco” is the more natural, verb-based way to say the same thing.
Lasciare + infinitive = to let someone do something. In the past it's essere-free: “hai lasciato” + bare infinitive.
Same lasciare + infinitive pattern — the pronoun “mi” sits before the verb.
“Lasciare entrare” = to let in — a super common fixed pairing you'll hear at doors and gates.
“Mai” slots between the verb and the infinitive — “non mi lasci mai...” wraps the negative.

cards.en: You don't let me do anything
cards.no: Italian needs the double negative — “non... niente,” never just “niente” after the verb.

cards.en: Why won't you let me do it?
cards.no: The object pronoun attaches to the infinitive — “far + lo” = “farlo,” not “lo fare.”

cards.en: He/she won't let me do it
cards.no: “Fare” + infinitive is the causative — literally “doesn't make me do,” used for “won't let me.”

cards.en: The light won't let me sleep
cards.it: La luce non mi fa dormire
cards.no: It's “la luce” (feminine singular), not “le luce” — and “fare” again = won't let me sleep.
Permettere always takes “di” before the infinitive — “permesso DI uscire.”

cards.en: The owner let me use the garage
cards.it: Il proprietario mi ha permesso di usare il garage
cards.no: Permettere needs an indirect object (mi/ti/gli) — “mi ha permesso di...” = allowed me to.

cards.en: They didn't allow me to enter
cards.it: Non mi hanno permesso di entrare
cards.no: Same permettere + di pattern, negated — contrast with “lasciare entrare” which drops the “di.”
Present tense of permettere — still “di” + infinitive, just a different subject.
Impersonal “è permesso” = it's allowed; “più” with “non” = not anymore.
It's “comprarlo” (comprare + lo), not “compralo”; “non... più” = not anymore.
Risolto = solved/resolved; superato = gotten past a problem.
Piccolo softens it — makes the advice feel low-pressure, not preachy.
Corrected 'se no sbaglio' to 'se non sbaglio' — sbagliare always needs 'non', not 'no'.

cards.en: Pass through the park (imperative) / go through the park (common)
cards.it: Passa attraverso il parco / Passa per il parco
cards.no: Per is the everyday choice; attraverso sounds a touch more formal/literal.

cards.en: I went through the park (most common) / more literal variant
cards.it: Sono passato per il parco / Sono passato attraverso il parco
cards.no: Per is what you would actually say; attraverso emphasizes going from one side to the other.
Both natural — camminata suggests a proper walk, due passi a short stroll.

cards.ex: Avevo paura che si rompesse (I was afraid it would break)
cards.no: Imperfect subjunctive (rompesse) matches a past-tense fear; potesse rompere is the more analytical alternative.
"Che X che c'è" is a common exclamatory pattern — not literal, just intensifies.
Dare da mangiare is the standard phrase for feeding an animal or person.

cards.en: Make sure to lock the door.
cards.it: Assicurati di chiudere la porta a chiave.
cards.no: Chiudere a chiave = to lock (with a key); assicurarsi di + infinitive = make sure to.

cards.ex: Ma chi ti credi di essere?
cards.no: Permettersi here = to take the liberty — used almost exclusively in this indignant expression.
Sdraiarsi and stendersi are interchangeable for lying down.

cards.en: The heat makes me want to lie down. The heat makes me sleepy.
cards.it: Il caldo mi fa venire voglia di sdraiarmi. Il caldo mi fa venire sonno.
cards.ex: Con questo caldo mi viene solo sonno.
cards.no: Fare venire voglia/sonno = "make [someone] feel like/sleepy" — a very common causative pattern.
-iamo ending on a reflexive verb = "let's" for a group action.
Corrected from 'si respir' — impersonal si + respirare, describes relief/breathing room.

cards.en: I'll try to do a bit without overdoing it
cards.it: Provo a fare un po' senza esagerare
cards.no: Corrected — provare needs 'a' before an infinitive, and it's esagerare not esaggerare.

cards.en: I feel like crying / it makes me feel like crying / it makes me hungry
cards.it: Mi viene da piangere / Mi fa venire da piangere / Mi fa venire fame
cards.no: Venire da + infinitive = "feel like doing" — one of the most useful causative constructions in Italian.

cards.en: Let's see first, worst case we'll ask for directions along the way
cards.it: Prima vediamo, al massimo chiediamo strada facendo
cards.no: "Strada facendo" = "along the way" — handy idiom, literally "the road doing."
Succedere and capitare are interchangeable for "to happen."

cards.en: there were a lot of them
cards.no: Ne stands in for "of them" — don't drop it, the sentence sounds incomplete without it.

cards.en: there are so many of them
cards.no: Tantissimi is the superlative of tanti — "so many," stronger emphasis.
Corrected 'apposto' to 'a posto' — two separate words.

cards.it: Il massimo risultato con il minimo sforzo
cards.ex: Il massimo con il minimo sforzo
cards.no: Corrected 'resultati' to 'risultato' and added the articles — Italian needs 'il' before massimo/minimo here.

cards.ex: È spenta (if referring to a device)
cards.no: Corrected 'E stacata' — needs the accent (È) and double 'c' (staccata).
Confusa agrees in gender/number with the subject — confuso if referring to a male/masculine noun.

cards.en: He/she didn't let you (plural) do it
cards.no: "Ve lo" = double clitic, indirect (to you-plural) + direct (it) object.

cards.ex: le è stata rubata la bicicletta
cards.no: Indirect object "le" (to her) + rubare — the standard way to say something was stolen from someone.

cards.en: I should do it as soon as possible
cards.no: "Il prima possibile" and "al più presto" are interchangeable for ASAP.

cards.en: You think so? / Do you think so?
cards.no: Ti pare (lit. "does it seem so to you") is a quick, skeptical way to question something.
Merenda specifically means an afternoon snack — a cultural staple, not just any snack.

cards.en: as soon as possible (or once possible); as much as possible — I try to save as much as possible
cards.it: il prima possibile (o appena possibile); il più possibile — Cerco di risparmiare il più possibile
cards.ex: Cerco di risparmiare quanto più posso
cards.no: Don't confuse "il prima possibile" (as soon as) with "il più possibile" (as much as) — easy to mix up.

cards.en: I would never allow myself (to do that)
cards.no: Permettersi in the conditional = "would allow oneself" — used for things you consider beneath/inappropriate for you.

cards.en: You’re often in a bad mood
cards.no: "Di cattivo umore" = in a bad mood; pairs with "di buon umore" for good mood.
Corrected — missing "a" before the infinitive; "fare a + inf" = to manage to do something.
"In fondo" = deep down/actually — fixed idiom, no productive slot to vary.
Corrected — "volta" pluralizes after "due": "due volte", not "due volta".

cards.en: I messed up — I think you’re screwed
cards.it: Ho fatto una minchiata, mi sembra che tu sia fregato
cards.no: Corrected "minciata"→"minchiata" (informal/slangy for blunder). FLAG: subject check — "tu" (you're screwed) reads oddly if it was your mistake; did you mean "io" (I'm screwed)?
“Ne” stands in for something already understood — a photo, a coffee, whatever came up before this line. Already natural, no correction needed.

cards.ex: Speriamo che vada per il meglio.
cards.no: “Speriamo per il meglio” is a literal calque of the English — Italians just say “speriamo bene” instead.

cards.en: As for me, I’m asking you...
cards.no: “Invece” contrasts with something someone else just said — natural as an opener, left as a fragment on purpose.

cards.en: I had no doubt about it.
cards.no: Corrected “non l’avevo dubbi” — dubbi is plural, so it needs “ne” (about it), not the singular “lo.”
Corrected “faceva calda assurda” — impersonal weather always uses “un caldo/freddo” (masculine noun), so the adjective has to agree: assurdo, not assurda.

cards.en: You can’t throw away the best part.
cards.it: La parte migliore non si può buttare via.
cards.ex: La parte più buona non si butta.
cards.no: “Migliore” reads more natural than “più buona” for “best”; “buttare via” (throw away) is the fuller everyday phrasing.
Corrected — “iniziare” always needs “a” before an infinitive.

cards.en: From now on, you’re allowed to have one friend.
cards.it: D’ora in poi ti è permesso avere un amico.
cards.ex: Da ora in poi puoi avere un amico.
cards.no: “D’ora in poi” and “da ora in poi” are interchangeable for “from now on.”

cards.en: From now on, you can’t have more than one friend with the same name.
cards.it: Da ora in poi non puoi avere più di un’amica con lo stesso nome.
cards.no: Added the accent — “piu” → “più.”

cards.en: Same for me, that works perfectly.
cards.it: Per me uguale, per me va benissimo.
cards.no: “Per me va bene/benissimo” is the everyday way to say something works for you.

cards.en: Would a place like this work for you all?
cards.no: “Andare” in the conditional + an indirect pronoun (vi/ti) is the go-to way to float a suggestion.

cards.it: I sogni di Jordan si sono realizzati.
cards.no: Flagging this one — guessed you meant “Jordan’s dreams came true,” fixed the spelling (realisato → realizzato) and swapped “da” → “di” for possession. If you meant something else, tell me and I’ll redo it.
Corrected the spacing — “prima dora” → “prima d’ora” (the apostrophe elides “di” + “ora”).
Stock connector for introducing a topic — goes straight into a noun, no extra preposition needed after “riguarda.”

cards.it: Non mi sento a mio agio.
cards.ex: Non mi sento a mio agio con lui.
cards.no: “Sentirsi a proprio agio” (feel at ease) — the possessive agrees with the subject: a mio/tuo/suo agio.
“Dovere essere stato + [participio]” is the standard way to guess about someone’s past state.
“Pretendere” is a false friend — it means “to demand/expect,” not “to pretend” (that’s fingere).

cards.en: In that case, you’d be right.
cards.no: “In quel caso” + conditional is the standard way to hedge an agreement.

cards.en: I don’t want any more of it.
cards.no: Added the accent to your alt phrasing — “cosi” → “così.” Both versions are natural; the first is the more common everyday one.
Kept as-is — the best translation depends on context (a sports shot vs. a literal hit), let me know if you meant something more specific.
“Nel modo giusto/sbagliato” — common adverbial phrase for describing how something’s done.

cards.en: By the way, thanks for the update.
cards.no: Corrected “into” → “intanto” (meanwhile/in the meantime) — likely autocorrect or a mishearing.

cards.en: Only like this, otherwise you can’t come in.
cards.it: Soltanto così, altrimenti non potete entrare.
cards.ex: Solo così, sennò non potete entrare.
cards.no: Added the accent — “cosi” → “così.”
“Entro” + a time period = “by/within” — entro la settimana, entro domani, entro fine mese.

cards.en: I ate some chicken Cameron made.
cards.it: Ho mangiato del pollo preparato da Cameron.
cards.ex: Ho mangiato il pollo che ha fatto Cameron.
cards.no: “Preparato da” (prepared by) is a touch more formal than the relative-clause alt — both are natural.

cards.en: How much do you miss it? / How much longer for you?
cards.no: “Mancare” does double duty: “ti manca” can mean “you miss it” or “you have X left” — context decides which. Flagging the ambiguity rather than guessing.
Corrected the article — “la entusiasmo” → “l’entusiasmo.” Entusiasmo is masculine (il/l’), even though it can feel like it should take “la.”

cards.ex: Senza che tu te ne accorga.
cards.no: “Senza che” always triggers the subjunctive — sappia, not sai.
“Grandezza” covers size/magnitude generally; “dimensioni” is more specific to physical measurements.

cards.en: I’m not used to someone doing that.
cards.it: Non sono abituato al fatto che qualcuno lo faccia.
cards.ex: Non sono abituato a queste cose.
cards.no: Completed the fragment — “abituato che” + subjunctive (faccia) is used when it’s someone else doing the thing, not you.

cards.en: How sure are you about it?
cards.no: “Sicura” agrees with a female subject — sicuro if you’re asking a man.

cards.en: A doubt just occurred to me.
cards.no: Added the accent — “mi e” → “mi è.” “Venire un dubbio/un’idea/una voglia” is the standard construction for something suddenly occurring to you.
“Processare” (to process, e.g. clearing an inbox) is common tech/business Italian borrowed from English — perfectly natural in that context.

cards.en: Just for a drink, we can sit down
cards.it: Giusto per bere qualcosa, possiamo sederci
cards.no: Giusto per = just for the sake of. Your original repeated “bere qualcosa” twice, so I trimmed it.
Casual and a bit blunt — fine with friends, can sound dismissive with someone you don’t know.

cards.en: I’ll think about it as I go — I’ll wing it
cards.it: Ci penso strada facendo, farò a braccio
cards.no: Strada facendo = along the way. A braccio = off the cuff, improvised.

cards.en: I didn’t do it on purpose
cards.no: Apposta is the everyday word; di proposito is a touch more formal.
Imperfect “volevo” softens the ask — the native way to open a question, not “voglio.”
Natives usually say mi sta piacendo or me lo sto godendo; amare is strong for things. “Questo lo” puts the emphasis up front.

cards.en: That’s not a short amount of time
cards.ex: È un bel po’ di tempo
cards.no: Non è poco = understatement meaning “quite a lot.” Works alone for any amount.

cards.en: If it’s not urgent, I can call you back
cards.it: Se non è urgente, ti posso richiamare
cards.ex: Se non è urgente, ti richiamo dopo
cards.no: Ri- prefix = back/again: richiamare. Say the full “non è urgente.”
